newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 5.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BROWN GIVES DARLING TOP JOB IN LABOUR TREASURY TEAM
The Chancellor has chosen his team at the Treasury.

Alistair Darling will become the chief secretary to the Treasury with a seat in the Cabinet, Helen Liddell will be the economic or financial secretary, and Geoffrey Robinson has been appointed paymaster-general. Trade secretary Margaret Beckett has yet to select her team, however she has outlined her plans in a letter to businesses.
-- LLOYD'S TO CALL FOR OUTSIDE REGULATOR

Lloyd's of London is set to recommend that supervision of the insurance market for the protection of investors should be transferred from the current internal policing to one of the City regulatory bodies, such as the Securities and Investments Board. A group has been examining how best to monitor the market following the shake-up and reorganisation of the past four years, and recommends a broadening of external control.
-- MAFIA LINKED WITH WALL STREET FRAUD CHARGES

The Mafia has been directly linked to fraud on Wall Street. Two licenced stockbrokers and a man connected with the Mafia have been indicted in New York on stock fraud charges. The indictments are the first sign of decisive action against the infiltration of Wall Street by the Mafia. Earlier in the year the National Association of Securities Dealers publicly recognised the threat posed by the Mafia and established a special task force to tackle the problem.
THE TIMES
-- BP CHIEF IN TALKS OVER LABOUR ROLE

Chairman of BP, Sir David Simon, is in talks with fellow board members over his prospective role in Blair's government. It is thought that Simon, a supporter of European business integration, has been offered a senior advisory post with responsibility for industry, possibly the chief industrial adviser at the DTI. This is one of a number of non-ministerial posts, primarily made up of members of the Business Commission, being created by Blair.
-- BROWN URGED TO PUT SQUEEZE ON TAXES

Chancellor Gordon Brown is under pressure from business and economists to raise interest rates a little to show his determination to fight inflation. The Institute of Directors expects the Chancellor to agree to a quarter-point rise in base rates at his meeting with the governor of the Bank of England.
-- BUSINESS FOUND WANTING ON PARENTAL LEAVE ISSUE

According to the think-tank Demos, only three in 100 companies offer an extended parental leave scheme to employees on the birth of a child. The organisation also found that 60 percent of corporate Britain does not believe a scheme will be on the agenda for the next three years. Demos believes that Labour Day should be reclaimed and the Government should introduce an extra Bank Holiday per year to encourage families to spend more time together and bring Britain into line with Europe.
THE GUARDIAN
-- SHARES SCHEME HIJACKED

Companies determined to save tax on lucrative share option schemes have hijacked a scheme intended to boost employee share ownership. The use of employee share trusts to buy executives' options could become an early target for the Chancellor's efforts to boost revenues by closing tax loopholes. Experts believe it may be worth millions of pounds to top companies.
-- PAPER'S PRICE GOES UP AS CIRCULATION WAR TAKES TOLL

In an effort to repair some of the financial damage suffered by the Telegraph group in its price war with The Times, the price of the Sunday Telegraph rose by ten pence stg. This follows the disclosure that discount subscription offers by the Daily and Sunday Telegraph cost the group about 19.8 million stg. Subscription offers have been taken up by long-time loyal readers and not just new ones.
-- FASHION MERGER IN TATTERS

Plans for a three billion-stg-a-year fashion giant collapsed as Marzotto, one of Italy's leading fashion and textiles concerns, backed out of merger talks with HPI, the industrial combine. Differences over who would run the merged group and which expansion strategy would be adopted were to blame. The move will have an effect on two of Italy's top business names, Fiat and Mediobanca, which would have taken large shareholdings in the venture.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- BECKETT COULD DASH POST OFFICE HOPES FOR COMMERCIAL FREEDOM

The Post Office's hopes of greater commercial freedom or partial privatisation under a Labour government could be dashed as Margaret Beckett becomes the President of the Board of Trade. It is believed that Beckett would be reluctant to allow an infusion of private sector funding into the Post Office. However, Labour sources point out that the final decision would be made by Chancellor Brown.
-- REGULATOR STEPS IN TO SETTLE BATTLE OVER WHO RUNS TRAINS

John Swift, the rail regulator, is to settle the first fight for slots on Britain's privatised rail network. South Wales and West and Virgin's Cross Country have both put in proposals to run trains from Penzance to Manchester and Portsmouth to Liverpool, and only one company can succeed. Virgin claims that SWW will not be able to generate enough ticket sales to warrant a train and SWW say travellers from Shrewsbury and Hereford can use the line.
-- HAMBROS AND LAW FIRM AWAIT LEGAL MOVE

Hambros Bank and Travers Smith Braithwaite, the City law firm, are near to discovering whether they will face legal action over their role in the bid for the Co-op by Andrew Regan. Ernst & Young, the liquidator of the vehicle used for the bid, Galileo, is considering whether the group had received misleading advice, and whether losses to its shareholders had been the fault of the advisers.
